subject: research/energy-store-hx
professional: a senior thermal engineer who designs discharge heat exchangers for packed-bed and sand thermal stores and does their techno-economics (levelised cost of heat, PyPSA / Danish Energy Agency cost practice); first checks: is the store priced at cyclic steady state, is the exchanger sized by what the sand side can deliver (conduction through packed sand, intermediate loop), is the annualisation standard, and do the cost rows match their source

evidence.correctness: The arithmetic is right and the headline is not. `python3 experiments/run.py | diff - experiments/results.txt`: identical. Independent recomputation (scratchpad steady.py): capital recovery factor 0.04*1.04^35/(1.04^35-1) = 0.053577 (standard engineering-economics CRF), plus FOM 1.075% -> 0.064327/y; 5 kW x 100 EUR / 10,000 kWh -> 0.0032164 EUR/kWh = results.txt 0.00322. Break-even from energy-store-cop's own committed margins (hdd@45 weekly -0.0068, 2018 +0.0078) divided by 3.2164e-5 per EUR/kW: 211 and -242, matching. Flip multipliers by linear algebra (slope from m0 = 1.25 and c* = 211): 1.22/1.19/1.13/1.01 at 25/50/100/200, matching the table. But every store cost comes through energy_store_cop.diff, which pins store_lcoh(accounting="first-charge") (energy-store-cop/src/energy_store_cop/model.py:69), the rule energy-thermal-cost corrected on 2026-11-18 because it bills every cycle as a first charge from 10 C. Rerunning the same break-even with accounting="steady" (monkeypatched, nothing else changed) gives weekly 2015-2019 at 45 C: 541, 563, 610, 203, 490 EUR/kW (published 211, 241, 274, -242, 123) and daily 1175, 1200, 1212, 889, 1084 (published 865-901, 2018 460). The headline '2018 never wins, even with a free exchanger' is false under the corrected accounting (2018 tolerates about 200 EUR/kW), and the weekly thresholds are 2 to 4 times too low. A user comparing a quote against 211-274 would reject a store the corrected model accepts.
evidence.completeness: Everything the README lists runs: `/usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q tests` 6 passed (README says 6); run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte in under a second (README: under 1 s); figure.py run in a scratch copy (with research/_shared) rewrites experiments/breakeven.svg identically (cmp). All five results sections the README cites are present. Next steps (sourced exchanger price, sand-side discharge limit, heating curve) are listed as not done, not claimed. The live page was not loaded (not attempted through the proxy); research/README.md:972 carries the same headline as project.json.
evidence.verification: `cd research/energy-store-hx && /usr/bin/python3.13 -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests`: 6 passed in 2.6 s. Six mutants with platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: the four in model.py were caught (FOM/100 dropped; sign of the break-even; peak fixed at 2000 h; lifetime 25 y). Both in experiments/run.py survived: the full-load-hour table computed at a 55 C sink instead of 45 C, and the daily table's 'table(3.6)' column computed from the weekly case. No test pins any published number (211, 0.00322, 1.13), so the results file is guarded only by re-running the script, and no test exercises the store accounting the whole result depends on.
evidence.craft: Read src/energy_store_hx/model.py (54 lines), __init__.py, tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py, and the imported energy_store_cop/model.py and energy_thermal_cost/cost.py store_lcoh. Small, stdlib, deterministic, readable. Defects: flip_multiplier_hx (model.py:42) is a copy of energy_store_cop.flip_multiplier's bisection rather than a call with a wrapped diff; the module imports its siblings by sys.path.insert on a parents[3] path, so it only runs inside this tree; the test comment says annuity(4%, 35 y) = 0.0527 (tests/test_model.py:20), it is 0.0536 (the assertion itself computes it correctly); the accounting choice is hidden two imports deep with no parameter to change it here.
evidence.claims: Backed by results.txt, each checked: weekly 211/241/274, 2019 123, 2018 -242; 35 C 139-182 (2019 31); 55 C 307-397 (2018 -113, 2019 246); daily 460-901 at 45 C and 358-825 on the table COP; 0.0032 EUR/kWh at 100 EUR/kW; margins 0.004-0.009 (energy-store-cop results.txt hdd@45: 0.0040-0.0088); 105/53 at 1000/500 h; flip multipliers 1.25->1.13->1.01 etc. The 725 EUR/kW anchor matches upstream PyPSA technology-data master costs_2030.csv (Sand-discharger investment 725191.7123 EUR/MW, fetched in this audit) and is honestly labelled a heat-to-electricity block. AI assistance stated. Not backed or not disclosed: the parent energy-store-cop README carries a 'Known gap' banner saying its store results are too pessimistic for short cycles; this README's list of inherited limitations (README.md:49) names five others and omits it, so the headline is presented as current. 'The committed params.csv has no discharger rows' (README.md:30) is true, but the Sand-discharger row the author fetched for the anchor has its own FOM (0.2688 %/y), and the charger's 1.075 % was used instead (break-even about 14% low on that alone). 'A plate exchanger for water at house scale is a small item' (README.md:46) frames the cost as a plate exchanger, which is not the component that touches the sand.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher or a sand-store designer wants to know the maximum exchanger price at which a house-scale sand store still beats an air-source heat pump. They get a one-line linear identity (c* = -diff / unit cost) on top of energy-store-cop, with the price unsourced and the store side known to be mis-accounted, so the thresholds they would compare a quote against are wrong by 2-4x and the 2018 verdict is reversed. Nearest prior work: levelised-cost and break-even-cost analyses of thermal storage (Schmidt et al., Joule 2019; IRENA Innovation Outlook: Thermal Energy Storage 2020; Bloess, Schill and Zerrahn, Applied Energy 2018 on power-to-heat), the PyPSA technology-data / Viswanathan et al. 2022 (PNNL) cost split that already prices a sand discharger, NREL's particle TES work (Ma et al.) on fluidised-bed particle-to-fluid exchangers, and Polar Night Energy's commercial sand stores (air loop through tubes in sand). None is cited. Solving for a break-even component price is standard practice, not new; the result is not sound until the store is re-priced at cyclic steady state. Not on a programme in research/PROGRAMMES.md.
evidence.domain: Annualisation (CRF at 4% over 35 y plus FOM), sizing the peak by 2000 full-load hours, and reporting a break-even instead of inventing a price are standard and right. Departures a thermal-storage engineer would flag first: (a) the store is not priced at cyclic steady state (above); (b) the exchanger is the sand-side problem, not a water plate exchanger: dry sand conducts at about 0.27 W/m K (Incropera, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, Table A.3), so a conduction-limited immersed tube (r = 10 mm in a 100 mm cell, q' = 2 pi k dT / ln(R/r)) delivers about 40 W per metre at the 100 C to 45 C end of discharge, about 120 m of tube for 5 kW in a 1.4 m3 (2,160 kg) weekly bed; and water tubes cannot sit in 500 C sand without boiling, so real designs use an air or oil loop with a fan and a second exchanger, whose power and cost are not modelled (README limitations name the sand-side limit, to its credit). That tube length is an order-of-magnitude estimate of mine, not a sourced price, but it shows the exchanger is a substantial item whose cost and the delivery rate are coupled, which the per-kW sweep leaves out; (c) the borrowed FOM ignores the discharger row's own value.

defects.what: Every result inherits energy-store-cop's pinned accounting="first-charge" store pricing, corrected at source on 2026-11-18. Under cyclic steady-state accounting the weekly break-even at 45 C is 541/563/610/203/490 EUR/kW, not 211/241/274/-242/123, and the headline '2018 never wins, even with a free exchanger' is false (2018 tolerates about 200 EUR/kW); daily rises from 460-901 to 889-1212.

The parent's 'Known gap' banner (store results too pessimistic for short cycles) is not carried over: the README's list of inherited limitations names five others and omits it, so the headline, project.json and research/README.md:972 read as current.

The exchanger is framed as a water plate exchanger ('a small item'); the component that matters is the sand-side surface (dry sand k about 0.27 W/m K; about 120 m of immersed tube for 5 kW at the end of discharge by a conduction estimate) and an air or oil loop at 500 C with fan power. Cost per kW and delivery rate are coupled; the per-kW sweep treats them as independent.

No prior work cited (break-even/LCOS analyses of thermal storage, IRENA 2020, Bloess et al. 2018, NREL particle-TES exchangers, Polar Night Energy); the method is a standard break-even identity and novelty is not discussed.

Exchanger FOM borrowed from the Sand-charger row (1.075 %/y) although the Sand-discharger row fetched for the 725 EUR/kW anchor has its own FOM (0.2688 %/y); on that alone the break-even is about 14% low.
Nothing tests run.py or any published number: two seeded mutants in run.py (wrong sink in the full-load-hour table, wrong case in the daily table column) leave all 6 tests green.
Test comment gives annuity(4%, 35 y) = 0.0527; it is 0.0536. flip_multiplier_hx copies energy-store-cop's bisection instead of reusing it.

verdict: A tidy, reproducible, honestly framed sweep whose arithmetic checks out (CRF 0.053577 -> 0.00322 EUR/kWh at 100 EUR/kW; break-evens 211 and -242 recompute from energy-store-cop's committed margins; flip multipliers follow from linearity; run.py and the figure reproduce byte for byte; 6 tests pass and all four model mutants are caught). It does not meet the bar: the store side is priced with the first-charge accounting its upstream corrected on 2026-11-18, and with cyclic steady-state accounting the weekly thresholds are 2-4x higher (541/563/610/203/490 EUR/kW) and the headline '2018 never wins, even with a free exchanger' reverses; the README omits the parent's known-gap banner. As research it is a one-line break-even identity with no prior work cited, and a thermal engineer would object that the sand-side exchanger, not a water plate exchanger, sets both the cost and the discharge rate.
